questiontext.text:
Consider the trigonometric equation \( {@eqn@}, \qquad 0^\circ \le \theta < 360^\circ. \)

You may use a calculator. Give angles in degrees, correct to \(1\) decimal place.

(a) Rearrange the equation to find the exact value of \(\cos\theta\), as a fraction.

\(\cos\theta = \) [[input:ansk]] [[validation:ansk]] [[feedback:prtk]]

(b) Determine the reference angle \(\alpha\).

\(\alpha = \) [[input:ans0]]\(^\circ\) [[validation:ans0]] [[feedback:prt0]]

(c) In which quadrants do the solutions lie?

[[input:ansq]] [[validation:ansq]] [[feedback:prtq]]

(d) Hence solve the equation for \(0^\circ \le \theta < 360^\circ\). You may give the two solutions in either order.

First solution: \(\theta = \) [[input:ans1]]\(^\circ\) [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
Second solution: \(\theta = \) [[input:ans2]]\(^\circ\) [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked solution

We are solving \({@eqn@}\) for \(0^\circ \le \theta < 360^\circ\).

(a) Rearranging the equation

Get \(\cos\theta\) on its own, just as you would solve \({@A@}y + \left({@B@}\right) = 0\) for \(y\).

Step 1: move the constant to the other side. \({@A@}\cos\theta = {@-B@}\).

Step 2: divide both sides by \({@A@}\).

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{ {@-B@} }{ {@A@} } = {@k@}. \]

(b) The reference angle

The reference angle \(\alpha\) is the acute angle whose cosine is the size of \(\cos\theta\), ignoring the sign. With the calculator in degree mode,

\[ \alpha = \cos^{-1}\left({@p/q@}\right) = {@alpha_disp@}^\circ \quad (\text{to 1 decimal place}). \]

(c) The quadrants

\(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point on the unit circle. \(\cos\theta = {@k@}\) is [[if test="is(s=1)"]]positive. By the CAST rule, cosine is positive in Quadrant I (All) and Quadrant IV (Cosine)[[else]]negative. By the CAST rule, cosine is positive only in Quadrants I and IV, so it is negative in Quadrants II and III[[/if]]. There is one solution in each of these quadrants.

(d) The solutions

    [[if test="is(s=1)"]]
  • Quadrant I: \(\theta_1 = \alpha = {@x1_disp@}^\circ\).
  • Quadrant IV: stop \(\alpha\) short of \(360^\circ\), \(\theta_2 = 360^\circ - \alpha = 360^\circ - {@alpha_disp@}^\circ = {@x2_disp@}^\circ\).
    • [[else]]
  • Quadrant II: stop \(\alpha\) short of \(180^\circ\), \(\theta_1 = 180^\circ - \alpha = 180^\circ - {@alpha_disp@}^\circ = {@x1_disp@}^\circ\).
  • Quadrant III: go \(\alpha\) past \(180^\circ\), \(\theta_2 = 180^\circ + \alpha = 180^\circ + {@alpha_disp@}^\circ = {@x2_disp@}^\circ\).
    • [[/if]]

Both angles lie in \(0^\circ \le \theta < 360^\circ\). Check with the calculator: \(\cos^{-1}\left({@k@}\right) = {@acosk_disp@}^\circ\), which is \(\theta_1\). For cosine, the other solution is always \(360^\circ - \theta_1\) (not \(180^\circ - \theta_1\), which is the rule for sine): \(360^\circ - {@x1_disp@}^\circ = {@x2_disp@}^\circ\).

Final answer:

\[ \theta = {@x1_disp@}^\circ \quad\text{or}\quad \theta = {@x2_disp@}^\circ. \]

On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate, so the solutions are where the vertical line \(x = {@k@}\) meets the circle. Both points make the reference angle \(\alpha\) with the \(x\)-axis:

questiondescription.text: Objective: solve trigonometric equations involving cosine for 0° ≤ θ < 360°. The cosine value is always a fraction (no surds); only cos θ = ±1/2 gives a special angle, so angles are given to 1 decimal place.

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

feedbackvariables.text: /* allow 0.06 for rounding to 1 decimal place */ gave_sol : is(abs(ans0 - x1) <= 0.06 or abs(ans0 - x2) <= 0.06);

truefeedback.text: Your answer looks like an angle in radians. Set your calculator to degrees and try again.

node.description: Gave a solution instead of the reference angle

truefeedback.text: That is one of the solutions of the equation, not the reference angle. The reference angle is the acute angle \(\cos^{-1}\) of the size of \(\cos\theta\), so it is less than \(90^\circ\). (For a negative cosine, \(\cos^{-1}\) on the calculator gives an obtuse angle.)

falsefeedback.text: Find \(\cos^{-1}\) of the size of your value from part (a) (ignore any minus sign), with the calculator in degree mode, and round to \(1\) decimal place.

truefeedback.text: Your angle is outside the range \(0^\circ \le \theta < 360^\circ\). Add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring it into the range.

node.description: Solution for the opposite sign, or used 180 - theta

truefeedback.text: That angle solves the equation with the opposite sign of \(\cos\theta\). A common slip is to use \(180^\circ - \theta\), which is the rule for sine. For cosine, the solutions are in the quadrants given by the CAST rule; if \(\theta_1\) is one solution, the other is \(360^\circ - \theta_1\).
Your answer is in radians. Give the solution in degrees.

node.description: Did not divide by the coefficient

truefeedback.text: You have moved the constant correctly, but \(\cos\theta\) is still multiplied by \({@A@}\). Divide both sides by \({@A@}\).

falsefeedback.text: Rearrange to get \(\cos\theta\) on its own: move the constant to the other side, then divide by the coefficient of \(\cos\theta\). Give the answer as a fraction.

feedbackvariables.text: sq : setify(ansq); onegood : is(cardinality(sq) = 1 and cardinality(intersection(sq, qset)) = 1);

node.description: The two quadrants for the opposite sign

truefeedback.text: Those are the quadrants where \(\cos\theta\) has the opposite sign. Check the sign of your value in part (a), then use the CAST rule: cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV.

node.description: Only one of the two quadrants

truefeedback.text: That quadrant is correct, but there is a second one. Cosine has the same sign in two quadrants: use the CAST rule to find the other.

falsefeedback.text: Use the CAST rule: cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV and negative in Quadrants II and III. Tick the two quadrants that match the sign of \(\cos\theta\).
